strategy.summary: Meridune is a sound, mid-sized private Chinese foundry and our cheapest source for Impeller HI 250 (40% quota; the German second source charges about half as much again). It has sold below our should-cost for years and cut its price in every renewal, recorded each time as 'below full cost to keep the volume'. It values cash: it asked for payment within days against a cash discount. Quality has turned around to zero complaints, while delivery is still below the contract target but around the peer median. We are a tiny customer to it, it owns the tooling and it can afford to walk. Further price pressure therefore has little room and real risk. The best results come from paying it in terms it values (faster payment, binding volume or quota, a 24-month commitment) so that any cost-recovery ask stays modest and supply stays secure. A new sales managing director has just been appointed, so expect a possible reset of positions.
strategy.decision_maker: Sales side of Meridune; a new managing director for sales was appointed recently (news:20260925-37). We do not know who holds pricing authority. Expect the new MD to want a visible early result, such as a cost-recovery increase or faster payment.

persona.owner_type: private, Co., Ltd., about 900 staff, mid-sized CN investment-casting foundry
persona.style: Operational, calendar-driven and pragmatic. Historically accommodating on price to keep volume; asks directly for what it needs (cash).
other_traits: small customer to it: our spend is about 0.1% of its turnover
owns the tooling for our part
quality recently turned around to zero ppm
strict holiday shutdown with early call-off deadlines
settles below its own ask in renewals

needs.detail: Wants faster payment and is willing to grant a cash discount for it. Our current terms are long net terms.
Has repeatedly accepted below-cost prices to keep the volume. Binding volume or a higher quota share is its core motive.
Its price is below should-cost, while alloy and labour drivers have risen. It needs cost recovery or at least no further cut.
Runs a long lead time, a holiday shutdown and early call-off deadlines. A longer commitment and timely call-offs help it plan.
Its quality improved from a red scorecard class to zero ppm, better than the second source. It will want this acknowledged.

constraints.detail: Its current price is below our bottom-up should-cost, which includes no margin. Every renewal note says it accepted below full cost. Should-cost confidence is low.
Its equity ratio is moderate and it actively asks for early payment against a discount. Its credit index is stable, so this is a cash preference rather than distress.
Price is fixed per calendar year, and a change needs written notice before year end within the notice period. The term auto-extends unless terminated with notice.
It owns the tooling. Moving its share to the second source means new tooling at a much higher unit price.
Long lead time and a holiday shutdown; on-time delivery is persistently below the contract target.

levers.why: Its own request for faster payment. Answering it with a concrete payment trade is the strongest, cheapest lever and shows we listen.
The shared forecast is up on actual orders. Volume is what it has always traded price for.
Anchors the current price as the base for any increase discussion.
The alloy surcharge has fallen recently, which tempers an alloy-driven increase claim.
Power is down over twelve months, a checkable offset to its cost claims.
An increase outside the annual notice window has no contractual basis; use this calmly on timing only.
Shows we are a reliable payer and supports a payment-for-price trade.
Shows it historically settles below its ask; use only as an internal guide or a light reference.
Delivery is below the contract target. Use it as a fresh-fact filler or to ask for a delivery commitment, not as a price weapon.
The quality agreement anchors the delivery target and complaint fee if performance terms come up.

trades.why: It values cash highly. Shorter payment buys price, or caps an increase, at small interest cost to us. Hold it back for the final round.
A longer commitment gives planning security and volume certainty. Extending to about 24 months captures that value; longer adds nothing.
Binding volume within our real need is its core motive. State it as binding in a single sheet.
Accept its standard lead time; asking for shorter would be priced steeply and strain a late-delivering plant.

Only if it insists on alloy exposure. A clause on the alloy surcharge at a price below the fixed price, without a deadband, can replace a fixed-price increase. The index is currently easing, so price the clause carefully.
For any increase, offer a later effective date against a slightly higher price as an alternative sheet.

price_view.reasoning: The price sits below our no-margin should-cost and has fallen in every renewal, with each event recorded as below full cost. Alloy and labour drivers have risen net of power, so a modest cost-recovery ask is justified and checkable. Should-cost confidence is low and the indices are German while the plant is in China, so the evidence is thin, but it all points the same way. The second source is far dearer and needs new tooling. The realistic goal is to keep any increase small by paying in terms, not to cut price.

do: Acknowledge the long relationship and its quality turnaround explicitly
Answer its payment request concretely in the first e-mail
Welcome the new sales MD and frame the deal as a stable partnership
Put verified figures on the table instead of asking about its costs
Plan call-offs around its shutdown and say so
dont: Do not demand a further price cut on a part it already sells below cost
Do not threaten to move volume to the second source
Do not ask open questions about its margin or cost structure
Do not push past a declared final offer

traps: Citing the rival price or rival quote (rival_price:310051:8d9d9659, rival_quote:310051:88fd1f2b) reveals that Meridune is far cheaper and strengthens its hand.
Citing should-cost (should_cost:310051:3146c8d4) proves it sells below cost and argues for an increase.
Using the price trend or early order history (price_trend:310051:c93d6b25, order_history:310051:7da8adc9) shows its past cuts and invites a catch-up ask.
The quality record (quality_record:all:564f546a) argues its case; mention it only as recognition.
The supplier-health record shows it can walk, and the dependency record shows we are a tiny customer; never invoke either against it.
The non-checkable peak arguments (index_peak:*) cost trust if cited.
The new-MD news is noise, not a lever.
Generic market news (copper, electronics, steel) is not about this part and would be rejected.
Threatening exit via the renewal notice risks losing our cheapest source, which owns the tooling.
The rising-alloy index arguments are for them; do not volunteer them.
Granting fast payment mid-negotiation without a price step wastes it.
strategy.writer_notes: Treat this as a supplier we need to keep healthy. Open warmly, reply to its payment request with a concrete faster-payment option tied to price, and confirm the shared forecast volume as a binding figure together with a longer term. Recognise the quality turnaround. If it asks for an increase, accept the principle that costs moved, show that power and the recent alloy fall offset part of it, and settle near cost recovery paid partly through terms. Keep its lead time. Ask for a delivery-reliability commitment as a soft extra, not a price argument. Never mention the second source's prices. Expect the new sales MD to test us early.
questions_to_ask: What cash discount would you grant for faster payment, and which payment term suits you best?
Would a binding annual volume and a longer contract help you plan capacity for this impeller?
What call-off timing around your holiday shutdown works best for your plant?
What would help you lift on-time delivery toward the contract target?
Do you buy alloy at fixed prices or at the monthly surcharge?

findings.text: Meridune sells part:310051 below our should-cost: EUR 79.44 vs EUR 84.97 (-6.5%). The should-cost has no margin in it, so the gap to a healthy price (cost plus about 5-8%) is roughly EUR 10-12. Confidence is only about 5%, but even at the bottom of that band (about EUR 80.7) the price is at or below cost. There is no room on price to push down.

Its price fell in every renewal: 85.96 (2023), 81.60 (-5.1%), 81.34 (-0.3%), 79.44 (-2.3%), so -7.6% since 2023. Notes on all 4 events say it accepted below full cost to keep the volume. Further cuts would deepen a loss-making position.

Cost drivers point slightly up since the last price. Labour LCI-C is +2.7% (weight 0.29, about +0.8% on price). Alloy AS-14404 is +5.9% (weight 0.24, about +1.4%). Power PPI-D351 is -3.7% (weight 0.09, about -0.3%). The net effect is about +1.9% on price, roughly EUR 1.5. AS-14404 has fallen 5.5% since its 2026-06 high, which tempers the alloy argument. Power is far below its peaks, but only the 12-month change is checkable.

The rival Feinguss Allgäu-Reiter (DE, 60% quota) is far dearer: EUR 118.73 now (+49.5%) and quoted 130.30 in rfq:6000000106. Meridune quoted 91.4 in that RFQ and still lost on lead time (112 vs 48 days). Meridune is our cheapest source, and the fallback price is much higher.

Any increase claim from Meridune is checkable and largely justified. A raise of about +2% from the indices, up to cost-covering (about +7%), is defensible. The cheapest compensation is non-price: shorter payment (it asked for 10-day payment with a discount on 2026-07-01), the volume growth from 1408 to 1483, or a longer term.
The should-cost confidence is low (5%) and the cost weights are category-team estimates. The indices are German, while the plant is in China, so the driver evidence is thin for a CN cost base.

supplier_wants: price increase toward full cost (about +2% index-based, up to about +7%)
faster payment (10 days with cash discount)
risks: Pushing price down further on a below-cost part may make it walk away: it is financially sound and we are about 0.1% of its turnover.
Fallback to sup:70180 costs about 50% more, plus new tooling.
If we stay below a healthy margin, the supplier-health charge applies.
AS-14404 is volatile; a fixed price accepted now could lag if alloy falls further.

useful_arguments.why: Anchors the current EUR 79.44 as the base for any increase.
Power -3.7% is a checkable offset against its claims.
Alloy has fallen 5.5% since June, which dampens an alloy-driven ask.
Rising volume is a trade we can offer instead of price.
It values cash, so faster payment is a cheap concession for us.
Shows we are a reliable, fair payer.
History shows it settles below its ask.

open_questions: What increase will Meridune actually ask for, and on which drivers?
Is a CN-specific labour/energy index available instead of the DE ones?
What does the 10-day payment discount cost us compared with the interest?
Can a longer term or a higher quota (from 40%) substitute for price?

findings.text: Evidence on decision-makers is thin: only two short operational e-mails and one news item. A new managing director for sales was appointed on 2026-09-25. Expect a new counterpart who may want an early visible win or a reset of positions. The record classes the news as noise, so it is no lever.

Meridune values cash. On 2026-07-01 it asked us to pay within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount. Our contract gives us 90 days net (our standard is 60), so faster payment is a tradeable concession it wants.

We are a reliable payer: 68 invoices, on average 2.5 days late in the last 12 months, never more than 7 days late, no discounts taken and nothing short-paid. However, 74.2% of invoices are paid slightly late. That may annoy a cash-focused supplier, but it is not a grievance on record.

The supplier is financially sound but not cash-rich: turnover EUR 39.3M, equity ratio 25.3%, credit index 254 and unchanged over 12 months, 900 staff, VDA 6.3 audit grade B. Our spend is about 0.1% of its turnover, so we are a small customer that it can afford to lose.

It already sells below cost. On four recorded events it accepted prices below full cost to keep the volume. The price has fallen 7.6% since 2023 and sits about 6.5% under should-cost, while the rival source charges about 49% more. Room for further cuts is limited, and pushing hard risks deprioritisation or a request for an increase.

It runs a strict operational calendar: the plant closes from 23 December to 6 January, and January call-offs are due by 10 December. Its 105-day lead time and FCA China delivery mean we must plan ahead.

Its quality has improved sharply: 0 ppm now against 5,254 ppm a year earlier. Delivery is 84% on time against a 95% target, roughly in line with peers. It will likely seek recognition for the quality turnaround.

supplier_wants: Faster payment (10 days) in exchange for a cash discount
To keep or increase volume and quota (currently 40%) on part 310051
Early call-offs around the holiday shutdown
risks: The below-cost price is unsustainable; it may demand an increase or deprioritise a small customer like us
The new sales managing director may reset positions or take a tougher line
It owns the tooling, so moving the part requires new tooling; the alternative source is far more expensive
Delivery at 84% is under target; the 105-day lead time and holiday shutdown add supply risk

Shows we are a reliable, fair customer

It has historically settled below its ask
Delivery is below the 95% target, a legitimate request for improvement
Prices are fixed per calendar year with 90 days' notice, which constrains any increase
The renewal and exit notice window gives us leverage on a longer commitment
The recent alloy surcharge fall counters any material-cost claim

What cash discount rate would it grant for 10-day payment?

findings.text: Framework agreement covers only Impeller HI 250, runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and auto-extends 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice (by 2027-04-01). The exit is still open and credible because a second approved source exists.

Price is fixed per calendar year. A change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, i.e. by about 2 October for 2027. Any 2027 increase demand must respect this; a late demand has no contractual basis.

Payment is 90 days net, against our standard of 60. FCA, 105-day lead time. Quality agreement: 95% on-time target, EUR 150 flat per complaint. The supplier asked in July 2026 for 10-day payment against a cash discount, so payment days are a tradeable currency it values.

History: in every renewal it settled below its own ask (avg ask -0.9%, settled -2.6%). The price fell from 85.96 to 79.44 (-7.6%) since 2023. All four events are noted 'accepted below full cost to keep the volume'. Should-cost is 84.97, so the current price is about 6.5% below cost. Further cuts are unrealistic and would raise the margin-health risk; a renewal is more likely to see a cost-recovery ask.

Dual sourcing: Feinguss Allgäu-Reiter (DE) holds a 60% quota and won the 2024 benchmark RFQ. Its price is far higher (118.73 currently, 130.30 quoted), so Meridune at 40% is our cheapest source. Shifting quota to the rival costs us roughly +50% per unit.

Mutual dependency is low on its side: we are about 0.1% of its turnover and it is financially sound. Meridune owns the tooling, so moving its 40% would require new tooling; the rival's tooling is ours. Volume is still the lever it values, as it repeatedly priced below cost for it.
Performance: 0 ppm (peers' median 457) but 84% on time against the 95% contractual target. The quality agreement gives us a delivery argument.

supplier_wants: Cost recovery: it is priced below full cost (alloy and labour arguments available to it)
Faster payment, ideally 10 days with a discount
Volume security or a higher quota share, and a longer commitment
Possibly an alloy index clause given AS-14404 volatility
risks: Pressing for further cuts on a below-cost price may make it walk away or degrade service; we are a negligible customer to it
Losing Meridune shifts volume to the ~50% dearer rival and needs new tooling
Citing rival prices reveals that Meridune is far cheaper and weakens us
A missed 90-day price-notice window for 2027 changes the timing of any price discussion

useful_arguments.why: The 90-day notice rule fixes the 2027 price unless properly notified
Exit is still open before 2027-04-01, which gives the renewal discussion weight
It has consistently settled below its own ask
Anchors at the current price of 79.44
Rising volume (1483 vs 1408) is something it values; offer it in trade
Its stated wish for faster payment gives us a trade currency against the 90-day term
84% on time vs the 95% contractual target
Counters alloy-surcharge increase claims with the recent fall
Energy cost is down 3.7%
We pay reliably

open_questions: Has Meridune sent a price-change notice for 2027 within the 90-day window?
Is a quota shift toward Meridune feasible given the rival owns no tooling risk and our tooling?
What is the part's category goal (stabilise vs leverage), which decides how much the below-cost margin matters?
Why is the 2024 RFQ award to the dearer rival recorded? Were there capacity or lead-time reasons (105 vs 48 days)?

findings.text: Delivery is the weak spot: rolling OTD has stayed between 72% and 84% against the 95% contract target for the whole two years. It recovered to 84% in the latest window (74.1% a year earlier). When late, it averages 14.5 days (max 21) in the last 12 months. The OTD gap below target is our main performance argument for better terms, but 84% is roughly the peers' median of 84.6%, so it does not argue for a lower price.

Quality has turned around. There were 4 supplier-caused QNs on part:310051 between 2024-07 and 2025-05 (porosity twice, burr, dimension), with ppm peaking at 7905 in 2025Q2 (class C, red). There have been zero complaints since 2025-05: 0 ppm in the latest window against a peers' median of 457 ppm, class A green, score 92. It now beats the second source sup:70180 (1182 ppm). This record argues the supplier's case.

The cost of poor performance to us has been small. Only EUR 150 was recharged across 4 QNs, and 3 complaints were not charged even though the contract allows a EUR 150 flat fee per complaint. 10 of 72 order lines were rush orders, against 2 of 73 at sup:70180, which suggests our planning compensates for its lateness.

Volume outlook is steady to slightly up. The 2026-09 forecast is 1483 pcs for the next 12 months against 1408 ordered, and the forecast is shared with suppliers. At its 40% quota that means roughly 590 pcs/yr for Meridune, similar to the 577 it received in the last 12 months. The forecast shows seasonal dips in December and August.

Price has fallen from 85.96 (2023) to 79.44 (2026), while our should-cost is 84.97. That is about 49.5% below what we pay sup:70180. Meridune is cheap and is selling below estimated cost, which weakens any push for further reductions.
Recent order lines were confirmed at the requested dates, so lead-time confirmation looks fine now. There are 7 open lines totalling 159 pcs.

supplier_wants: Faster payment, with a cash discount offered in return (today's terms are 90 days)
Recovery of a price that is below cost, using alloy surcharge and labour increases as justification
risks: Pushing hard on price while it sells about 6.5% below should-cost could make it walk away. We are only about 0.1% of its turnover, it is financially sound, and it owns the tooling.
Losing it would shift volume to sup:70180 at about EUR 118.73, roughly 40 EUR/pc dearer.
Delivery unreliability (16% late, up to 21 days) combined with a 105-day lead time and the year-end plant closure creates supply risk.
Citing the sup:70180 price would reveal that Meridune is far cheaper than its rival.

useful_arguments.why: 84% OTD against a 95% target justifies a delivery commitment or performance terms in exchange for any concession.
The contract sets the 95% OTD target and the EUR 150 complaint fee, which anchor performance terms.
Rising shared forecast volume is something we can trade.
The current price of 79.44 anchors any increase.
The recent alloy surcharge fall counters claims that material costs are rising.
Energy prices are down 3.7% over 12 months.
It values cash, so faster payment can be traded for price or delivery terms.
We pay reliably, which shows we are a fair customer.

open_questions: What is the root cause of late deliveries, and is the 84% recovery sustainable? The evidence is a single-part view.
Should we start charging the EUR 150 complaint fee consistently?
How much of our rush ordering is caused by its lateness rather than by our own planning?
Can sup:70180 absorb more volume if Meridune is lost?

arguments.text: Our price is already below our full cost: the customer's own bottom-up estimate of our plant puts unit cost at EUR 84.97 with no margin, against our current EUR 79.44. We have cut the price in every renewal since 2023 (85.96 to 79.44, -7.6 %) to keep the volume. There is no room for a further cut, and we need a modest recovery.

We are by far the cheapest source. Feinguss Allgäu-Reiter charges EUR 118.73, about 49 % more. In the 2024 benchmark they quoted 130.30 against our 91.40. Moving our 40 % share to them costs the customer roughly EUR 23k a year.
Our quality has turned around. We have had zero complaints and 0 ppm for the last 12 months, and our scorecard is now class A at 92. The second source had 1,182 ppm and a complaint in July 2026.

Material cost has risen. The alloy surcharge for our grade family is up 5.9 % year on year, steel is up 7.3 % since January, and alloy weighs about 24 % of our cost. I will avoid power, which fell, and copper, which does not apply to us.
We own the tooling. A shift of share needs new tooling and a new qualification at the customer's expense.
Delivery is improving: 84 % on time over the last 12 months, up from 72 %. Late deliveries are often rush call-offs; 10 of our order lines were rush orders.

weak_points: On-time delivery is still well below the 95 % contract target, and we were 16.5 days late on average when late.
Our scorecard was red (class C) for four quarters in 2025-26, so the quality turnaround is only about a year old.
The cost indices are German (labour, power), while our plant is in China. German labour +2.7 % does not describe our cost.
The should-cost confidence is only 5 %, and we keep offering cuts, which suggests our margin is better than we claim.
Our 105-day lead time, plus the holiday shutdown, creates a planning burden for the customer.
We asked for faster payment, which reveals our cash needs. With a 25 % equity ratio, they may read this as weakness.
Under the contract, a price change needs 90 days' notice before year end, so the timing for 2027 is tight (notice by early October).
The customer is small for us (about EUR 45k a year), so a threat to walk away is believable but costly in goodwill.
wants: Payment in 10-30 days instead of 90; we would grant about a 2 % cash discount for it.
A binding annual volume of about 1,450-1,500 pcs, or a higher quota (50 %+).
A 24-month price commitment and contract extension.
An index clause on the alloy surcharge instead of a fixed price, if no increase is possible.
Firm call-offs by the deadline before the holiday shutdown, and fewer rush orders.
In return: hold the price flat at 79.44, or limit the increase to 1-2 %.
red_lines: No higher complaint chargeback or a ppm penalty without volume in return.
No transfer of tooling ownership for free.
No shorter lead time than about 90 days without paid air freight.
Once our final offer is stated, we will not move again.
red_team.opening: Thank them for the long partnership, and point to our zero-ppm, class A record and the price cuts we have absorbed for four years. Ask for +4.5 % for 2027 (about EUR 83.00), still well below their cost estimate and the German source, citing the alloy and steel increases. Signal right away that we can hold close to the current price if they pay within 30 days, commit to about 1,450 pcs a year (or 50 % quota) and extend the contract for 24 months.

rebuttals.answer: We respect that you have supported this impeller with sharp prices over the years, and we are not asking for a further cut. Our estimate is a rough bottom-up view with wide uncertainty, so we read it as a sign that a healthy price is close to today's level, not as proof of a specific gap. Today's price is the natural base for our talks. Rather than a price step, we would like to help you through terms you value: faster payment, a binding volume in line with our shared forecast and a longer commitment.

You are a competitive and valued source, and we want to keep it that way. We run a dual-source set-up for supply security, not to play one partner against the other, and we will not discuss another supplier's commercial terms. What matters between us is a fair price for your share and reliable supply, and we would like to strengthen your position with a binding volume.

Your quality turnaround is real and we appreciate it. Your team has clearly done good work. Please understand that it follows a period with a red scorecard, so it is still recent. We see sustained performance as the basis of a longer partnership, rather than as grounds for a price increase. We would gladly reflect it in a longer commitment.

We agree that alloy is higher than a year ago. But the surcharge has eased again in recent months, and power has fallen over the year, which offsets part of the rise. General steel prices cover a different product family from your grade. Taken together, the net movement is modest. If alloy exposure is your concern, we are open to discussing a fair clause on the alloy surcharge instead of a fixed increase.

That is true, and it is one reason we see you as a long-term partner rather than a supplier to replace. We have no plan to move your share, and we would like to confirm that with a binding volume and a longer term that also protect your investment in the tooling.

We see the improvement and welcome it. On-time delivery is still clearly below the contract target, however, and when deliveries were late, the delay was substantial. We accept that some rush call-offs were ours. In return, we will plan call-offs around your shutdown and lead time, and we would ask for a firm commitment to move toward the agreed target.

press: Could you share how you would move on-time delivery closer to the target in our quality agreement, given that late deliveries are still quite late when they happen?
As the indices on the table reflect German labour and power, we would welcome your view on how they apply to a plant in China.
We would like to answer your request for faster payment concretely, and would be glad to hear which payment term and cash discount suit you best.
Because prices are fixed per calendar year under our agreement, we suggest we settle any change for the coming year within the agreed notice process.
To ease planning around your lead time and holiday shutdown, we propose agreeing a call-off schedule together with a binding annual volume.
